Family Health

Penile cancer: symptoms, stages, treatment and support

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Penile cancer is an uncommon cancer of the skin or tissues of the penis. Most cases are squamous cell cancers. A new lump, sore or skin change often has another explanation, but needs assessment rather than a diagnosis from its appearance. Earlier assessment can give more treatment options.

Changes to get checked

Arrange a medical appointment promptly for a new or persistent lump, ulcer, rash, skin thickening, colour change or bleeding on the penis. Changes often affect the glans or foreskin but can occur elsewhere. Unusual or unpleasant-smelling discharge, itching, burning, difficulty retracting the foreskin or a groin lump also deserve review. Do not wait four weeks before asking about a concerning change.

These symptoms can come from inflammation, infection or other conditions as well as cancer. A referral to a specialist does not confirm cancer. If you cannot pass urine at all, seek immediate emergency care; this can be dangerous regardless of its cause. Embarrassment should not prevent care: you can ask about privacy, a chaperone and how an examination will be done.

Risk factors without blame

Anyone with a penis can develop penile cancer, although it is more common at older ages. Some cancers are associated with HPV, while others are not. Smoking, a tight foreskin called phimosis, long-term inflammation and some conditions or treatments that reduce immunity can increase risk. Having a risk factor does not mean you will develop cancer, and its absence does not exclude it.

Phimosis and smegma are not sexually transmitted infections. Smegma is a collection of shed skin cells and oils; it is not itself a proven cancer-causing substance. Having a foreskin, HPV or cancer is not evidence of poor character or a partner's infidelity. Ask about gentle hygiene, treatment for painful or tight foreskin, stopping smoking and HPV vaccination according to local eligibility. Condoms reduce some HPV exposure but cannot prevent every infection.

Examination, biopsy and selected tests

A clinician examines the penis and both groins. A biopsy removes a sample for laboratory examination and is central to confirming the diagnosis and identifying the cancer's features. Ask about pain relief, the procedure and when results will arrive. MRI or ultrasound may help assess depth when this affects treatment; CT, PET/CT or lymph-node sampling may be needed in selected circumstances.

Cystoscopy looks inside the urethra and bladder; it is not a routine test for spread throughout the body. Normal scans or no palpable groin lumps cannot exclude microscopic lymph-node disease. Depending on the tumour's risk, the specialist may discuss a sentinel-node biopsy, other node surgery or surveillance. Enlarged groin nodes can also reflect infection, so the team uses examination and appropriate sampling rather than assuming every lump is metastatic cancer.

What the stage describes

The TNM system describes the primary tumour (T), regional lymph nodes (N) and distant spread (M). The following is a simplified stage-group guide; grade and microscopic features matter. Stage 0 includes carcinoma in situ, called penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN), or a non-invasive verrucous tumour, without nodal or distant spread. Stage I is T1a: invasion into tissue beneath the surface with lower-risk microscopic features, N0 M0. It is not simply surface-only disease.

Stage II has no nodal or distant spread: IIA includes higher-risk T1b invasion or T2 invasion into the corpus spongiosum; IIB involves the corpora cavernosa (T3). Stages IIIA and IIIB combine a T1–T3 tumour with N1 or N2 regional nodal disease respectively, without distant spread. Stage IV includes invasion into other adjacent structures (T4), N3 regional disease or distant metastasis. Stage IV does not always mean distant spread.

Why groin-node assessment matters

Clinical and pathological nodal categories differ. On pathology, N1 means one or two involved groin nodes on one side; N2 means three or more on one side or involved nodes on both sides. Pelvic-node involvement or cancer extending outside a node is N3. You cannot assign these categories by counting lumps yourself. Ask whether the stage is based on examination and scans or on tissue examined after surgery.

Nodal assessment and treatment are a separate part of the care plan, even when the penile lesion is small. Decisions balance the risk of hidden spread against the complications of node procedures. Specialist experience matters in this uncommon cancer. Ask what tests are recommended, what uncertainty remains and whether review by a specialist multidisciplinary team or a second opinion would help.

Treating superficial disease

Non-invasive disease has not grown into deeper tissue; invasive disease has, but is not automatically present in lymph nodes or distant organs. For selected PeIN or superficial lesions, options can include prescribed topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, local excision, circumcision for suitable foreskin lesions, glans resurfacing or laser treatment. The choice requires an appropriate diagnosis and discussion of recurrence and side effects.

Topical chemotherapy is different from chemotherapy that circulates through the body. Do not use cancer creams, wart treatments or freezing products on an undiagnosed lesion. Cryotherapy is described among possible treatments, but evidence in PeIN is limited and it is not a standard solution for every lesion. Treatment response needs review; persistent or recurrent changes can require biopsy or a different approach.

Surgery can sometimes preserve the penis

Selected localised invasive cancers can be treated with organ-preserving surgery, such as wide local excision or removal of part or all of the glans with reconstruction. Removing cancer with adequate margins must be balanced with urinary and sexual function and the risk of recurrence. Invasion alone does not mean that everyone needs removal of the entire penis.

Partial penectomy removes part of the penis; total penectomy may be needed when a large or advanced tumour cannot be adequately treated with a smaller operation. Urination may then be redirected through an opening in the perineum. Reconstruction can be discussed but is individual and cannot guarantee previous appearance, sensation or sexual function. Ask about wound care, activity, pain, urinary changes and when to seek help.

Radiotherapy and treatment for more advanced cancer

External-beam radiotherapy or brachytherapy, which places a radiation source close to the tumour, can be options for selected localised cancers. Radiotherapy can also be used in other treatment settings or to relieve symptoms. Possible effects include skin changes, scarring and urinary or sexual problems; discuss these alongside surgical options rather than assuming one approach is always less harmful.

Cancer involving nodes or more extensive disease may need a combination of node surgery, systemic chemotherapy and sometimes radiotherapy. Chemotherapy can be given before or after surgery in selected circumstances. For advanced cancer, the specialist can explain current systemic options, clinical trials and whether a treatment aims to cure, control disease or ease symptoms. Palliative care can help manage pain and support wellbeing alongside cancer treatment.

Follow-up and outlook are individual

Keep the follow-up plan agreed with your team. It depends on the original tumour, lymph-node findings and treatment; there is no universal appointment interval for everyone. Follow-up can include examination of the penis and groins, selected scans or biopsies, and support with treatment effects. Report a new lesion, groin lump or other concerning change between visits rather than waiting for the next appointment.

Early localised disease is often treatable, but recovery cannot be guaranteed. Outlook depends particularly on nodal involvement, as well as tumour features, overall health and response to treatment. A population five-year survival figure is not a personal prediction or a limit on lifespan. Ask your specialist to explain your own results and the benefits and uncertainties of the proposed plan.

Support for daily life and relationships

Cancer and its treatment can affect body image, intimacy, erections, urination, fertility concerns and emotional wellbeing. Ask a specialist nurse or clinician about psychosexual support, counselling, rehabilitation and practical or financial assistance. With your consent, a trusted person can join appointments; peer groups may help, but you decide what to share. Intimacy and personal worth are not defined by one body part or performance.

BeMama can help organise questions, appointments and symptoms to discuss with your team. It cannot assess a lesion, confirm a biopsy result, assign a stage, select cancer treatment or predict survival. A photograph or app record must not delay examination. If recording intimate information, consider your privacy and the service's settings; bring the information you choose to share to a clinician.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Prompt examination and biopsy can distinguish cancer from other penile conditions; symptoms and photos cannot assign a diagnosis.

Staging includes depth and microscopic risk, lymph nodes and distant spread; clinical and pathological nodal categories are not interchangeable.

Organ preservation, node care, radiotherapy, systemic treatment and follow-up require individual specialist discussion, with urinary, sexual and emotional support.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to prepare questions, keep appointment dates and note changes for your cancer team. It cannot diagnose a penile lesion, interpret tissue or scans, assign stage, choose treatment or predict survival. Do not delay examination or urgent care to record symptoms or upload a photograph.

When to seek help

Arrange prompt clinical assessment for new or persistent penile sores, lumps, skin changes, bleeding, unusual discharge or groin lumps. Complete inability to pass urine needs immediate emergency care. Do not apply cancer creams, wart medicines or freezing products to an undiagnosed lesion. Follow specialist advice for treatment complications and new symptoms between appointments; an app cannot provide cancer clearance.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • New penile sores, lumps or skin changes need prompt examination; appearance alone cannot diagnose cancer.
  • Biopsy and risk-based assessment of the tumour and lymph nodes guide staging and treatment.
  • Some invasive cancers can receive organ-preserving treatment; treatment and follow-up are individual.
  • Urinary, sexual and emotional support matter, and BeMama cannot replace specialist assessment.

Frequently asked questions

What may be the first sign?

A lump, ulcer or change on the glans or foreskin can be an early sign, but cancer has no single diagnostic appearance. Rash, thickened or discoloured skin, bleeding or unusual discharge also need assessment. Ask promptly about a concerning change rather than waiting for it to become painful or large.

Who is more at risk?

Risk rises with age and can be associated with HPV, smoking, phimosis, chronic inflammation or reduced immunity. Not all cancers are HPV-related. A foreskin or a risk factor does not establish the diagnosis, and phimosis and smegma are not STIs. Risk discussions should support care, not blame.

How is penile cancer diagnosed?

Examination and a biopsy are central. Further imaging or lymph-node tests depend on the findings and risk. A cystoscopy is not a routine whole-body staging test, and normal scans do not rule out microscopic nodal spread. Ask when and how you will receive results.

Is stage I only on the surface?

No. Stage 0 includes surface-confined in-situ disease. Stage I describes T1a invasion beneath the surface with lower-risk microscopic features and no regional nodes or distant spread. The specialist should explain the exact TNM and grade rather than relying on a simplified label.

Does invasive cancer always require total penectomy?

No. Selected localised invasive tumours can receive organ-preserving surgery or other suitable treatments. Partial or total penectomy is needed in some situations to control cancer adequately. Discuss margins, recurrence, follow-up, urinary and sexual effects, and reconstruction with the specialist team.

Are cancer creams the same as systemic chemotherapy?

No. Prescribed topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod can treat selected superficial disease after diagnosis. Systemic treatment is used in different circumstances, including some nodal or advanced cancers. Do not self-treat an unexplained genital lesion with creams or freezing products.

Do survival statistics tell me how long I will live?

No. They describe groups treated in particular periods, not an individual's lifespan. Stage, lymph nodes, tumour biology, health and treatment response affect outlook. Ask your team what the findings mean for you, including uncertainty and available support.

When should I seek help before my next appointment?

Report new penile or groin changes promptly and follow the team's instructions for treatment complications. Complete inability to pass urine requires immediate emergency care. BeMama can keep questions and dates, but cannot decide whether a lesion, stage or treatment is safe.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
